definitions.explanation: A respectful way to refer to the Buddha or Buddhist deities. The さま suffix adds reverence.
A respectful, euphemistic way to refer to a person who has died. Rooted in the Buddhist belief that the deceased becomes a buddha. Common in conversation about funerals and death.

examples.japanese: {仏様|ほとけさま}に{手|て}を{合|あ}わせた。
examples.english: I pressed my hands together in prayer to the Buddha.

examples.japanese: {祖母|そぼ}は{毎朝|まいあさ}{仏壇|ぶつだん}の{仏様|ほとけさま}にお{茶|ちゃ}を{供|そな}えていた。
examples.english: My grandmother offered tea to the Buddha at the household altar every morning.

examples.japanese: {困|こま}った{時|とき}の{仏様|ほとけさま}{頼|だの}みでは{遅|おそ}い。
examples.english: It's too late to pray to Buddha only when you're in trouble.

examples.japanese: {仏様|ほとけさま}のお{顔|かお}はとても{穏|おだ}やかだった。
examples.english: The face of the deceased looked very peaceful.

examples.japanese: {仏様|ほとけさま}に{花|はな}を{手向|たむ}けた。
examples.english: I offered flowers to the deceased.

examples.japanese: {葬儀|そうぎ}の{際|さい}、{仏様|ほとけさま}の{思|おも}い{出|で}を{語|かた}る{時間|じかん}が{設|もう}けられた。
examples.english: At the funeral, time was set aside to share memories of the deceased.

notes:
USAGE:
The plain form {仏|ほとけ} exists but {仏様|ほとけさま} is far more common in spoken language due to the reverence associated with both meanings. In sense 2, it is a gentler alternative to direct words for death.

CULTURAL NOTE:
In Japanese Buddhism, it is believed that the deceased become buddhas, which is why the same word is used for both meanings. This connection shapes many Japanese funeral customs.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {仏様|ほとけさま}に{祈|いの}る (to pray to Buddha)
- {仏様|ほとけさま}を{拝|おが}む (to worship Buddha)
- {仏様|ほとけさま}のような{人|ひと} (a person as kind as Buddha — an extremely kind person)
